meta.trial_name: SPARCL (Stroke Prevention by Aggressive Reduction in Cholesterol Levels)
meta.mechanism: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (high-intensity statin); lowers LDL-C by about 43% vs placebo (mean during trial 73 vs 129 mg/dL)
meta.indication: secondary stroke prevention after a recent (1-6 months) stroke or TIA in patients without known coronary heart disease and LDL-C 100-190 mg/dL
meta.readout_date_note: SPARCL was first presented at the European Stroke Conference on 2006-05-17, but no readable release from that day exists (the conference abstract has no results; Pfizer issued no release until 2006-08-09). The readout date is therefore the first readable public announcement, Pfizer's release of 2006-08-09; expert commentary (the NEJM editorial) appeared from 2006-08-10, after the cut-off.

n_randomized.quote: Of 6670 screened, eligible patients, 4731 (70.9 percent) fulfilled the inclusion criteria and underwent randomization (Figure 1).
n_randomized.note: 2365 atorvastatin, 2366 placebo (Fig. 1). Registry S3 and the ESC abstract S5 give 4732.

median_followup.quote: The median duration of follow-up was 4.9 years (range among survivors, 4.0 to 6.6).

primary_endpoint.value: Time from randomization to a first nonfatal or fatal stroke (any type: ischemic, hemorrhagic or unclassified)
primary_endpoint.quote: The primary outcome was the time from randomization to a first nonfatal or fatal stroke.
primary_endpoint.note: Hemorrhagic strokes count toward the primary end point, so the hemorrhagic excess on atorvastatin is inside the primary HR.

inclusion_key_criteria.value: Age >18; ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke or TIA 1-6 months before randomization; modified Rankin <=3; LDL-C 100-190 mg/dL; no known coronary heart disease; atrial fibrillation and other cardiac embolic sources excluded
inclusion_key_criteria.quote: Eligible patients were men and women over 18 years of age who had had an ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke or a TIA (diagnosed by a neurologist within 30 days after the event) 1 to 6 months before randomization.
inclusion_key_criteria.location: Methods, Study Hypothesis and Patient Population
inclusion_key_criteria.note: Also: 'The exclusion criteria, which have been described in detail previously, included atrial fibrillation, other cardiac sources of embolism, and subarachnoid hemorrhage.' Entry events: ischemic stroke 67.4%/65.9%, hemorrhagic stroke 1.9%/2.0%, TIA 29.9%/31.8% (Table 1).

planned_events.quote: Given the specified statistical power, the enrollment of 4200 patients, and an assumed annual rate of 3.5 percent for the primary end point in the placebo group, the study was designed to continue until 540 primary end points had occurred.

assumed_rrr.quote: The study was designed to have a statistical power of 90 percent to detect an absolute reduction of 25 percent in the primary end point in the atorvastatin group as compared with the placebo group during a median follow-up of five years with a two-sided significance level of P<0.05.
assumed_rrr.note: Worded as an 'absolute reduction of 25 percent', which reads as a 25% relative (hazard) reduction; the ESC abstract S5 says '90% power to detect a 25% hazard reduction'. Recorded as RRR 0.25.

power.quote: The study was designed to have a statistical power of 90 percent

alpha.quote: Because of these interim analyses, the final P value had to be less than 0.048 to indicate a significant difference.
alpha.note: Nominal two-sided 0.05; seven interim efficacy analyses (P=0.0001 first, P=0.001 thereafter).

stopped_early.quote: Seven interim analyses of efficacy were performed during the study, with a stopping boundary corresponding to a two-sided significance level of P=0.0001 for the first analysis and P=0.001 thereafter.
stopped_early.note: Not stopped early; the ESC abstract S5 says 'The target number of patients with a primary endpoint has been reached and SPARCL is in the final stages of closeout.' Last visits March-June 2005 (S1).

baseline.note: Atorvastatin 132.7, placebo 133.7 mg/dL (means +/- SE; corrected footnote S21). Value = simple average of the two arms (derived). ~3.44 mmol/L. Table text read from the NEJM PDF (pdf.js text layer).
Simple average of the two arms (derived).
Simple average of the two arms (derived).
Simple average of the two arms (derived). On-treatment apoB is not reported.
Not reported. DERIVED as total cholesterol minus HDL-C of the arm averages (211.9 - 50.0).
Simple average of the two arms (derived).
NOT FOUND: not reported in the main paper.

biomarker_effects.method: LDL-C method not stated in the main paper
biomarker_effects.quote: The mean lipid values during the course of the trial were as follows: LDL cholesterol, 72.9±0.5 mg per deciliter (1.89±0.01 mmol per liter) in the atorvastatin group, as compared with 128.5±0.5 mg per deciliter (3.32±0.01 mmol per liter) in the placebo group (P<0.001)
biomarker_effects.note: Placebo-adjusted values DERIVED from the arm means: -55.6 = 72.9 - 128.5; -43.3% = -55.6/128.5. Intention-to-treat contrast: includes non-adherence and open-label statin use (placebo arm 25.4% took open-label statins; net difference in statin use 78.1%).

biomarker_effects.quote: Another explanation may be the larger reduction in LDL cholesterol in our study than in the HPS (56 mg per deciliter [1.4 mmol per liter] vs. 39 mg per deciliter [1.0 mmol per liter]).
biomarker_effects.note: -1.43 mmol/L DERIVED from the reported arm means 1.89 vs 3.32 mmol/L; the authors round it to 1.4 mmol/L (56 mg/dL). SPARCL is not in the CTT 2010 individual-data meta-analysis (S12).

biomarker_effects.quote: One month after randomization, the LDL cholesterol level in the atorvastatin group had decreased to 61.3±0.4 mg per deciliter (1.58±0.01 mmol per liter) (a decrease of 53 percent, P<0.001) and was unchanged in the placebo group at 133.5±0.5 mg per deciliter (3.45±0.01 mmol per liter) (P=0.65).
biomarker_effects.note: Early on-treatment contrast (before drop-outs and drop-ins). Placebo-adjusted values DERIVED: 61.3 - 133.5 = -72.2 mg/dL; -72.2/133.5 = -54.1%. The 53% is the within-arm change from baseline.

biomarker_effects.method: DERIVED as total cholesterol minus HDL-C
biomarker_effects.quote: high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, 52.1±0.3 as compared with 51.0±0.3 mg per deciliter (1.35±0.01 vs. 1.32±0.01 mmol per liter), respectively (P=0.006); total cholesterol, 147.2±0.6 as compared with 208.4±0.6 mg per deciliter (3.81±0.02 vs. 5.39±0.02 mmol per liter), (P<0.001)
biomarker_effects.note: Not reported by the trial. DERIVED: non-HDL-C 95.1 (147.2-52.1) vs 157.4 (208.4-51.0) mg/dL; difference -62.3 mg/dL = -1.61 mmol/L (x0.02586); -39.6%.

biomarker_effects.quote: and triglycerides, 111.5±1.3 as compared with 145.0±1.3 mg per deciliter (1.26±0.01 vs. 1.64±0.01 mmol per liter), respectively (P<0.001).
high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, 52.1±0.3 as compared with 51.0±0.3 mg per deciliter (1.35±0.01 vs. 1.32±0.01 mmol per liter), respectively (P=0.006)

biomarker_effects.note: NOT FOUND: only baseline apoB is reported (Table 1).
NOT FOUND: on-treatment blood pressure not reported in the main paper.

biomarker_effects.quote: Plasma LDL cholesterol reductions from baseline were dose related, with 25% to 61% reduction from the minimum dose to the maximum dose of 80 mg atorvastatin once a day.
biomarker_effects.note: Phase 2 dose-response (n=81, placebo arm included), published 1995. Change from baseline at 80 mg, not placebo-subtracted.

hr.quote: After prespecified adjustment for baseline factors, atorvastatin was associated with a 16.0 percent relative reduction in the risk of nonfatal or fatal stroke (hazard ratio, 0.84; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.71 to 0.99; P=0.03) (Table 2 and Figure 2).
hr.note: Prespecified Cox model adjusted for region, entry event, time since entry event, sex and age. Unadjusted log-rank P=0.05. Per-protocol (n=4162) HR 0.82 (0.69-0.98). Table 2: fatal stroke 0.57 (0.35-0.95); nonfatal stroke 0.87 (0.73-1.03), P=0.11; stroke or TIA 0.77 (0.67-0.88); major coronary event 0.65 (0.49-0.87); major cardiovascular event 0.80 (0.69-0.92), P=0.002; death 1.00 (0.82-1.21), P=0.98. Post hoc cause-specific: ischemic stroke 0.78 (0.66-0.94), hemorrhagic 1.66 (1.08-2.55).

ci_low.quote: hazard ratio, 0.84; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.71 to 0.99

ci_high.quote: hazard ratio, 0.84; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.71 to 0.99

p.quote: adjusted hazard ratio, 0.84; 95 percent confidence interval, 0.71 to 0.99; P=0.03; unadjusted P=0.05
p.note: Below the final threshold of 0.048 only in the prespecified adjusted model; the unadjusted log-rank P was 0.05.

events_treatment.unit: patients with a first fatal or nonfatal stroke (atorvastatin, N=2365)
events_treatment.quote: During a median follow-up of 4.9 years, 265 patients (11.2 percent) receiving atorvastatin and 311 patients (13.1 percent) receiving placebo had a fatal or nonfatal stroke

events_control.unit: patients with a first fatal or nonfatal stroke (placebo, N=2366)
events_control.quote: 311 patients (13.1 percent) receiving placebo had a fatal or nonfatal stroke

safety_signals.value: Hemorrhagic stroke increased: 55 vs 33 patients; post hoc cause-specific HR 1.66 (1.08-2.55); fatal hemorrhagic stroke 17 vs 18
safety_signals.quote: The cause-specific adjusted hazard ratios in the atorvastatin group, as compared with the placebo group, were 0.78 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.66 to 0.94) for ischemic stroke, 1.66 (95 percent confidence interval, 1.08 to 2.55) for hemorrhagic stroke, and 0.55 (95 percent confidence interval, 0.21 to 1.40) for unclassified stroke.
safety_signals.note: Abstract conclusion: 'despite a small increase in the incidence of hemorrhagic stroke.' Fatal hemorrhagic stroke: 'The incidence of fatal hemorrhagic stroke did not differ significantly between the groups (17 in the atorvastatin and 18 in the placebo group).' Pfizer S2: 2.3% vs 1.4%.

safety_signals.value: Hemorrhagic-stroke risk factors (post hoc): atorvastatin HR 1.68 (1.09-2.59); hemorrhagic entry event HR 5.65; male sex HR 1.79; age HR 1.42 per 10 y; stage 2 hypertension at last visit HR 6.19; no relation to achieved LDL-C
safety_signals.quote: In addition to atorvastatin treatment (HR 1.68, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.59, p = 0.02), Cox multivariable regression including baseline variables significant in univariable analyses showed that hemorrhagic stroke risk was higher in those having a hemorrhagic stroke as the entry event (HR 5.65, 95% CI 2.82 to 11.30, p < 0.001), in men (HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.84, p = 0.01), and with age (10 y increments, HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.74, p = 0.001).
safety_signals.note: Goldstein et al., Neurology 2008 (epub 2007-12-12). 'There were no relationships between hemorrhage risk and baseline low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol level or recent LDL cholesterol level in treated patients.'

safety_signals.value: Across statin trials the hemorrhagic-stroke excess is non-significant (CTT: RR 1.12, 0.93-1.35 per mmol/L; 1.21, 1.05-1.41 with SPARCL and CORONA added); meta-analysis of 23 RCTs: RR 1.10 (0.86-1.41)
safety_signals.quote: If the published data for haemorrhagic stroke from SPARCL and CORONA were combined with the present meta-analysis then the rate ratio would be 1·21 (95% CI 1·05–1·41) per 1·0 mmol/L LDL cholesterol reduction.
safety_signals.note: CTT goes on: the absolute hazard 'would be about 50 times smaller (perhaps a few extra haemorrhagic strokes annually per 10 000 treated) than the definite absolute benefits'. Hackam 2011 (S13): 'Statins were not associated with an increased risk of intracerebral hemorrhage in randomized trials (risk ratio, 1.10; 95% confidence interval, 0.86-1.41)'. TST 2020 (S14): intracranial hemorrhage 'did not differ significantly between the two groups'.

safety_signals.value: Persistent ALT/AST >3x ULN: 51 (2.2%) vs 11 (0.5%), P<0.001; no liver failure
safety_signals.quote: Persistent elevation of alanine or aspartate aminotransferase (>3 times the upper limit of the normal group on two consecutive occasions) was more frequent in the atorvastatin group (51 patients, or 2.2 percent) than in the placebo group (11 patients, or 0.5 percent; P<0.001 by the chi-square test). There were no cases of liver failure.

safety_signals.value: No excess myopathy or rhabdomyolysis: myalgia 5.5% vs 6.0%; rhabdomyolysis 2 vs 3; AE-related discontinuation 17.5% vs 14.5%; serious AEs 41.8% vs 41.2%
safety_signals.quote: There were five cases of rhabdomyolysis, two in the atorvastatin group and three in the placebo group.
safety_signals.note: Table 3 (PDF text layer): Myalgia 129 (5.5) vs 141 (6.0); Any adverse event resulting in discontinuation 415 (17.5) vs 342 (14.5).

safety_signals.value: No mortality benefit: 216 vs 211 deaths, HR 1.00 (0.82-1.21), P=0.98; cancer deaths 57 vs 53
safety_signals.quote: The overall mortality rate was similar, with 216 deaths in the atorvastatin group and 211 deaths in the placebo group (P=0.98), as were the rates of serious adverse events.
safety_signals.note: 'The study was not powered to assess the effect of treatment on the risk of death from any cause'.

genetics.finding: Mendelian randomization: HMGCR (statin target) LDL-lowering variants protect against cardiovascular events, the same per unit LDL-C as PCSK9 variants
genetics.effect: OR 0.81 (0.72-0.90) per 10 mg/dL lower LDL-C for the HMGCR score
genetics.quote: Variants in PCSK9 and HMGCR were associated with nearly identical protective effects on the risk of cardiovascular events per decrease of 10 mg per deciliter (0.26 mmol per liter) in the LDL cholesterol level: odds ratio for cardiovascular events, 0.81 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.74 to 0.89) for PCSK9 and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.72 to 0.90) for HMGCR.

genetics.finding: LDL-C is causal for ischemic stroke, specifically large-artery atherosclerotic stroke, but not shown for small-vessel or cardioembolic stroke (MR)
genetics.effect: OR 1.12 (1.04-1.20) ischemic stroke and 1.28 (1.10-1.49) large-artery stroke per 1-SD genetically higher LDL-C
genetics.quote: A 1-SD genetically elevated LDL cholesterol was associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke (odds ratio: 1.12; 95% confidence interval: 1.04-1.20) and large artery atherosclerosis stroke (odds ratio: 1.28; 95% confidence interval: 1.10-1.49) but not with small artery occlusion or cardioembolic stroke in multivariable MR.

genetics.finding: Genetically higher LDL-C is associated with LOWER risk of intracerebral hemorrhage, i.e. LDL-lowering itself may raise ICH risk (supports an on-target explanation of the SPARCL hemorrhagic signal)
genetics.effect: OR 0.59 (0.42-0.82) for ICH per 1 mmol/L genetically higher LDL-C
genetics.quote: MR analyses indicated that 1mmol/L (38.67mg/dL) increase of genetically instrumented total and LDL cholesterol were associated with 23% (OR = 0.77; 95% CI = 0.65-0.98; p = 0.03) and 41% lower risks of ICH (OR = 0.59; 95% CI = 0.42-0.82; p = 0.002), respectively.

genetics.finding: CTT individual-data meta-analysis: LDL-lowering reduces ischemic stroke (RR 0.79 per 1 mmol/L) with a non-significant excess of hemorrhagic stroke (RR 1.12); all strokes -16% per mmol/L
genetics.effect: Ischemic stroke RR 0.79 (0.74-0.85); hemorrhagic stroke RR 1.12 (0.93-1.35) per 1.0 mmol/L LDL-C reduction
genetics.quote: Taking all 26 trials together, the risk reduction was 16% (95% CI 11–21; p<0·0001; webappendix p 8 ) per 1·0 mmol/L LDL cholesterol reduction, with a highly significant reduction in ischaemic stroke (1427 vs 1751; RR 0·79, 95% CI 0·74–0·85; p<0·0001; webappendix p 9 ) and a non-significant excess of haemorrhagic stroke (257 vs 220; RR 1·12, 95% CI 0·93–1·35; p=0·2; webappendix p 10 ).

consensus_explanation.summary: SPARCL met its primary end point: in patients with a recent stroke or TIA and no known coronary disease, atorvastatin 80 mg lowered mean LDL-C from 129 to 73 mg/dL and reduced fatal or nonfatal stroke from 311 to 265 patients (adjusted HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.71-0.99, P=0.03; unadjusted P=0.05; 5-year absolute reduction 2.2%), with larger reductions in major coronary events (HR 0.65) and major cardiovascular events (HR 0.80). The stroke benefit was at the edge of significance and modest in absolute terms (the NEJM editorialist called it 'relatively modest'), partly because hemorrhagic strokes, which count in the primary end point, rose from 33 to 55 (post hoc HR 1.66, 1.08-2.55) while ischemic strokes fell (HR 0.78), and because about a quarter of placebo patients took open-label statins. The investigators and later reviews judged the net effect clearly favourable and consistent with LDL-C lowering on an atherosclerotic, genetically validated target (HMGCR), and it changed practice (statins after ischemic stroke or TIA); the hemorrhagic signal was linked to prior hemorrhagic stroke, age, male sex and uncontrolled hypertension rather than achieved LDL-C, and meta-analyses (CTT 2010, Hackam 2011) found at most a small absolute excess of brain hemorrhage, so the caveat is caution in patients with prior intracerebral hemorrhage rather than a reversal of benefit.

open_questions: Readout date: the first public topline was the oral presentation at the 15th European Stroke Conference (Brussels), abstract 1 of 'New clinical trials I' on Wednesday 17 May 2006 (S5). No press release or other announcement dated that day could be found or read: Pfizer's archived 2006 US release index has no SPARCL release before 2006-08-09 (S2), the conference site's oral-session page for that session was not archived, and the earliest readable report is heartwire on 2006-05-23 (S6).

Placebo-adjusted lipid changes are derived from per-arm means (LDL-C 72.9 vs 128.5 mg/dL = -55.6 mg/dL, -43.3%; authors round to 1.4 mmol/L). The contrast is intention-to-treat and diluted by non-adherence and open-label statins (placebo 25.4% vs atorvastatin 11.4% open-label statin use; net difference in statin use 78.1%).
non-HDL-C is not reported; -1.61 mmol/L (-39.6%) is derived from total cholesterol minus HDL-C. On-treatment apoB, SBP and Lp(a) not reported.
Significance of the primary end point depends on the prespecified adjusted model (adjusted P=0.03 vs final threshold 0.048; unadjusted log-rank P=0.05).
